passage: At the science centre's summer workshop, Anirban, nine, finished the paper-rocket task in four minutes and spent the rest of the hour reading the adult display about black holes. Then his rocket's left fin came out slightly crooked. He crushed the whole thing and sat with his arms folded, blinking hard. At lunch the other children played tag in the courtyard; Anirban stood at the edge, pretending to read. Himani, the workshop leader, sat beside him. "Your questions about black holes were brilliant. And crooked rockets still fly." She held out her hand. "Come, they need one more for tag." He hesitated, then ran in. Ten minutes later he was the one shrieking loudest.

qa.q: What did Anirban read after finishing his rocket?
qa.a: He read the adult display about black holes.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel when his rocket's fin came out crooked?
qa.a: He felt upset and frustrated, wanting it to be perfect; he crushed it and sat blinking hard.

qa.q: What did Himani do that nurtured Anirban as a whole child?
qa.a: She praised his questions, gently eased his need for perfection and helped him join the game of tag with other children.

qa.q: How might the other children see Anirban once he joined tag?
qa.a: They may see him as a fun playmate, not just the boy who reads adult displays.

grounding: Shows a child with an advanced mind who is bored, perfectionistic and on the edge of play, and an adult who nurtures his need for friends and comfort.

passage:
Monday: Jasleen, eight, finished her Class 3 maths sheet in five minutes, then sighed loudly and drew spirals all over the back. "It's boring, Ganga Ma'am."
Thursday: Jasleen got one question wrong in the maths olympiad practice paper, out of forty. She hid under the library table and sobbed. "I'm not clever any more."
The next Tuesday: Ganga Ma'am gave her a book of logic puzzles for early finishers, and at break she walked her out to the playground. "Puzzles later. Hopscotch now." Jasleen hopped the whole grid twice with Noor and came back pink-cheeked, laughing about a sparrow that landed on square six.

qa.q: How many questions were on the olympiad practice paper?
qa.a: There were forty questions on the paper.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel after getting one question wrong?
qa.a: She felt crushed and scared that she was not clever any more, hiding and sobbing under the library table.

qa.q: What did Ganga Ma'am do that cared for Jasleen beyond marks?
qa.a: She gave her puzzles for deeper challenge but also sent her to play hopscotch with a friend, looking after her need for fun and friends.

qa.q: How might Noor experience playing hopscotch with Jasleen?
qa.a: Noor probably simply enjoyed a laughing playmate, and may not even think of Jasleen as different.

grounding: Shows a child far ahead in maths who is bored and perfectionistic yet still needs play and friends, and a teacher who nurtures the whole child.

passage: "Lavanya, you want to know what your Amma was like at your age? At nine she was reading her uncle's college chemistry book on the bus. I was so proud, I thought only of marks. More books, more tests. Then one evening I found her crying behind the water tank on the terrace. 'Nobody wants to play with me, Amma. They say I talk like a teacher.' I sat with her there till the lights came on. The next week I stopped the extra tests and took her to the colony's dance class. She was terrible at it! She laughed the whole time. That was when she made her first real friend, your Revathi Aunty." Vinita patted Lavanya's hand.

qa.q: What was Lavanya's Amma reading on the bus at nine?
qa.a: She was reading her uncle's college chemistry book.

qa.q: How was the young girl feeling when she was found behind the water tank?
qa.a: She felt lonely and hurt, crying because nobody wanted to play with her and they said she talked like a teacher.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vinita's story?
qa.a: After finding her daughter crying, Vinita sat with her, stopped the extra tests and took her to dance class, caring for her friendships, not only her marks.

qa.q: How might the girl in the story have felt at the dance class?
qa.a: She probably felt free and happy, laughing even though she was terrible at it, and finally found a real friend.

grounding: An elder recalls a gifted daughter who was lonely and felt different, and how turning from marks to play and friendship nurtured the whole child.

subtype: Teacher noticing a restless bright child [Observer]
passage: "Varun, you're frustrated with that boy who keeps disrupting your class? Let me tell you about Mukul, my old student. He finished every sum before I'd written the last one on the board. Then he'd ask, 'Ma'am, if there are infinite stars, why is the sky dark?' I didn't know! Then he'd throw paper balls at the fan. At first I gave him two extra worksheets. He threw more paper balls. So one day I said, 'Mukul, that sky question is a real puzzle. Find out, and teach it to us on Friday.' He spent the week in the library. On Friday he taught us with a torch and a steel plate. No paper balls. More sums was the mistake; a bigger question was the answer." Sunaina poured the tea.

qa.q: What did Mukul use when he taught the class on Friday?
qa.a: He used a torch and a steel plate.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel when Mukul asked his star question?
qa.a: She was surprised and a little stumped, since she didn't know the answer, but she came to respect the question.

qa.q: What choice inside the story changed Mukul's behaviour?
qa.a: Sunaina stopped giving extra worksheets and instead asked him to research his own question and teach it, giving depth instead of more work.

qa.q: How might Mukul have felt when asked to teach the class?
qa.a: He probably felt respected and excited, because his question was taken seriously and he had a real challenge.

grounding: An elder teacher recalls a restless bright pupil who finished early, asked deep questions and then disrupted, and how depth rather than extra work kept him engaged.

subtype: Teacher noticing a restless bright child [Observer]
passage: With the other teacher absent, Tenzin had two classes squeezed into one room, sixty-eight children, and the fans rattling. Wasim, ten, finished the fractions task in three minutes. "Sir, why can't you divide by zero? What actually happens?" Before Tenzin could answer, Wasim was drumming on the desk, and the back row joined in. Tenzin's first thought was to hand him another page of fractions. Instead he crouched by the desk. "Good question. Here's a bigger one. How would you split sixty-eight children into fair teams for the quiz? Show me three ways." Wasim grabbed his notebook. The drumming stopped. Ten minutes later he had four ways, and a note: "Divide by zero is like splitting sweets among no children. Ask me later."

qa.q: How many children were in the room?
qa.a: There were sixty-eight children in the room.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling as the drumming spread?
qa.a: He was likely stressed and tempted to hand Wasim more fractions, with a crowded, noisy room to control.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin's choice work better than extra worksheets?
qa.a: He respected Wasim's question and gave him a deeper, real problem to solve, which kept Wasim interested instead of bored.

qa.q: How might Wasim have felt when Tenzin called his question good?
qa.a: Wasim probably felt valued and eager, which is why he grabbed his notebook and stopped drumming.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a pupil who finishes early, asks probing questions and disrupts, and responding with depth and respect instead of more work, despite a crowded room.

subtype: Teacher noticing a restless bright child [Observer]
passage: In her Delhi classroom, Gurpreet Ma'am watched Eshaan, eight, finish the clock worksheet first again. "Ma'am, who decided a minute has sixty seconds? Why not a hundred?" She smiled, said "Good question, later," and gave him another worksheet. Within minutes he was flicking erasers at the fan. Gurpreet sighed and wondered if she had got it wrong. At break she sat with him and wrote his question on a card. "Your job this week: find out who first counted in sixties. Tell the class on Friday." Eshaan's eyes went wide. On Friday he explained, with drawings, how people long ago counted in sixties on their finger joints. The erasers stayed in his pencil box all week.

qa.q: What did Eshaan ask about minutes?
qa.a: He asked who decided a minute has sixty seconds, and why not a hundred.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel when Eshaan started flicking erasers?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and doubtful, sighing and wondering whether her extra worksheet had been the wrong move.

qa.q: What worked better than giving Eshaan another worksheet?
qa.a: Taking his question seriously and turning it into a research task he could share with the class, which added depth, not workload.

qa.q: How might Eshaan's classmates see him after his Friday talk?
qa.a: They may see him as someone with fascinating ideas instead of the boy who throws erasers.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a bright pupil who finishes early, asks probing questions and disrupts, and finding that depth and respect for questions work better than extra work.

passage: In their small town near Pala, everyone knew Thomas had topped the district exams. At cricket, the boys called him "Professor," not kindly. So in class he started leaving easy questions blank, hoping to seem normal. At home he redid every test paper, terrified that a single 98 would mean he was slipping. He felt alone in both places. Vidya Teacher, who ran the town library's evening astronomy group, stopped him one day. "Come on Saturday. Four others your age are building a telescope." He went. They argued about moons till nine at night, and nobody called him Professor. Walking home, Vidya said, "You know you're allowed a B sometimes?" Thomas laughed, and something in his chest let go.

qa.q: What did the boys at cricket call Thomas?
qa.a: They called him "Professor," not kindly.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel about his results before joining the astronomy group?
qa.a: He felt terrified and alone, worried a single 98 meant he was slipping, while also hiding his ability to fit in.

qa.q: What helped ease the strain on Thomas?
qa.a: Meeting like-minded peers in the astronomy group and hearing from a mentor that he was allowed a B sometimes.

qa.q: How does Vidya seem to see Thomas?
qa.a: She sees a bright boy who is lonely and under too much pressure, and wants him to have friends and room to be ordinary.

grounding: Shows a gifted teenager out of step with peers, hiding ability and afraid of not being top, relieved by like-minded peers, a mentor and permission to be average.

passage: In Gothenburg, Beatriz, fourteen, had started getting a few quiz answers wrong on purpose. When she scored full marks, the girls at her table went quiet and stopped inviting her to the café after school. At home she cried over a B in handball class, as if it proved something. Her maths teacher noticed the pattern and introduced her to Anders, who ran a maths circle on Thursday evenings at the university. The first night, a boy argued with her about a proof for twenty minutes, and she walked out grinning. At dinner her mother said, "A B in handball is just fine. You don't have to be first in everything." Beatriz stopped faking wrong answers. She had somewhere she belonged now.

qa.q: Who ran the maths circle Beatriz joined?
qa.a: Anders ran the maths circle on Thursday evenings at the university.

qa.q: How did Beatriz feel when her friends stopped inviting her after full marks?
qa.a: She felt lonely and left out, which is why she began getting answers wrong on purpose.

qa.q: What two things relieved the pressure on Beatriz?
qa.a: Finding peers who enjoyed arguing about proofs, and her mother telling her that a B in handball is fine.

qa.q: How might Beatriz's mother feel seeing her daughter cry over a handball grade?
qa.a: She may feel worried and sad that Beatriz believes she must be first in everything, which is why she reassures her.

grounding: Shows a gifted teenager hiding ability to belong and fearing any result that is not top, relieved by like-minded peers, a mentor and permission to be average.

passage: At two in the morning, the house master at the residential school, Suraj Sir, found Ira in the common room redoing a lab report. "It got 18 out of 20," she said, not looking up. "I lost two marks." Her eyes were red. Ira, sixteen, had few friends in the hostel; the others found her intense. Suraj Sir sat down. "Ira, you are allowed to be ordinary sometimes. Eighteen is fine. Sleep is not optional." The next week, he introduced her to three seniors preparing for the science olympiad, who met in the library after dinner. At the first meeting she laughed at a physics joke only they got. That night she slept straight through.

qa.q: What mark did Ira get on the lab report?
qa.a: She got 18 out of 20.

qa.q: How was Ira feeling at two in the morning?
qa.a: She was anxious and upset about losing two marks, redoing the report with red eyes.

qa.q: What did Suraj Sir do that relieved Ira's strain?
qa.a: He gave her permission to be ordinary, insisted she sleep and introduced her to like-minded seniors.

qa.q: How might the olympiad seniors see Ira after the first meeting?
qa.a: They may see her as one of them, someone who laughs at the same physics jokes, not as too intense.

grounding: Shows a gifted teenager who feels out of step and that every result must be top, relieved by like-minded peers, a mentor and permission to be ordinary.

passage: After I won the state quiz at thirteen, Baba lined up all my trophies in the drawing room, where every guest could see them. Every dinner was about the next rank. When I got 88 in chemistry, Baba didn't shout. He just went quiet for two days. That silence hurt more than anything. I started thinking that I was only worth loving when I won. One night I told him, shaking, "Baba, do you like me, or just the trophies?" His face changed. He took me for a long walk by the lake and said, "I love you, Bidisha. Not the trophies." Now on Sundays we cycle, and we have a rule: nobody mentions marks. I still work hard. I just don't feel afraid any more.

qa.q: What mark did Bidisha get in chemistry?
qa.a: Bidisha got 88 in chemistry.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel during Baba's two days of silence?
qa.a: Bidisha felt deeply hurt and afraid, believing love came only with winning.

qa.q: What change helped protect Bidisha's well-being?
qa.a: Baba said clearly that he loved Bidisha, not the trophies, and they started Sunday cycling with a rule of no talk about marks.

qa.q: How might Baba have felt when asked if he liked the trophies more?
qa.a: He was likely shocked and sad to learn his pride had made his child feel loved only for winning.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose proud parent pushes constant achievement, who feels loved only for brilliance, and how valuing the child beyond ability protects well-being.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 11, Wednesday.
Jeevan came in today saying he had not slept. He topped the pre-board but his mother asked why the maths was 97, not 100. He said, "Mum only smiles when I win something." He plays guitar in the school band, but she calls it a waste of revision time.
I asked his permission to call his mother in. She came this afternoon. When I read her his words, she cried and said she was only proud of him. We talked about how he hears it. We agreed on one evening a week with no talk of marks, and she said she would come to the band's performance on Saturday.
Next: check in with Jeevan on Monday. — Mehak

qa.q: What did Jeevan get in maths in the pre-board?
qa.a: He got 97 in maths.

qa.q: How does Jeevan feel about his mother's pride?
qa.a: He feels anxious and unloved except when winning, saying his mum only smiles when he wins something.

qa.q: What steps did Mehak take to help Jeevan?
qa.a: Mehak asked Jeevan's permission, met his mother, shared how he hears her pride and agreed a weekly evening with no talk of marks.

qa.q: How did Jeevan's mother react to hearing his words?
qa.a: She was hurt and shocked, crying and saying she was only proud of him, then agreed to value him beyond marks.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose proud parent pushes constant achievement so he feels loved only for results, and how valuing him beyond ability helps.

passage:
Sunday
Relatives over for lunch. Papa told everyone I'll crack the top engineering exam, "no question." He said it three times. Chacha asked what I like doing and I didn't know what to say.
Later Thomas came over and we were laughing at his cartoon of our physics sir. Papa came in and said, "No time for friends this year." Thomas left in two minutes.
I sat in my room and cried. I wanted to shout: am I just a rank to you? 
Then at night Papa knocked. He saw my face. He sat on the bed and said, "I've been so proud I forgot to ask about you. What do you like?" I said drawing. He got out my old sketchbook from the loft. We looked at it together till eleven.
Pradeep

qa.q: What did Papa take out from the loft?
qa.a: He got out Pradeep's old sketchbook from the loft.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel after Thomas left?
qa.a: Pradeep felt hurt and trapped, crying and wondering if Papa saw only a rank.

qa.q: What did Papa do at night that protected Pradeep's well-being?
qa.a: He admitted he forgot to ask about Pradeep, asked what Pradeep likes and spent time looking at the sketchbook together.

qa.q: How might Thomas have felt being sent away?
qa.a: Thomas may have felt awkward and unwelcome, and perhaps worried about his friend.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose proud parent pushes for constant achievement, making love feel tied to rank, and a parent who begins valuing the child beyond ability.

passage: In the small town of Malerkotla, Dilnaz, twenty, ran the numbers for her family's dairy cooperative. She could spot a cheating supplier from one column of figures. But she forgot meeting dates, lost the receipt book twice, and when her cousin Farhan came to her upset about failing his driving test, she said, "Just practise the reversing. It's simple." He walked out. That night she felt ashamed, twice over. Her aunt said, "You are sharp as a knife, Dilnaz, and sometimes you cut." Instead of sulking, Dilnaz made a wall calendar with coloured pins. Then she went to Farhan's room. "I was blunt. I'm sorry. Tell me how it felt?" He looked surprised, then started talking.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz make to handle her forgetfulness?
qa.a: She made a wall calendar with coloured pins.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel that night, and why?
qa.a: She felt ashamed twice over, for being disorganised and for hurting Farhan with a blunt reply.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz do that shows working on gaps without shame?
qa.a: She accepted her aunt's point, made a practical calendar and apologised to Farhan, asking how he felt.

qa.q: How might Farhan have felt when Dilnaz came to apologise?
qa.a: He was surprised and probably relieved and cared for, which is why he started talking.

grounding: Shows a young adult brilliant at analysis who struggles with organisation and emotional skills, and works on both without shame.

passage: In a student flat in Copenhagen, Lars, twenty-one, solved problem sets his physics professor called "graduate level." He also missed the deadline to register for his own exams, because the email sat unread among two hundred others. The same week his flatmate Yosef's grandmother died. Lars listened for ten seconds and started explaining how to book the cheapest flight. Yosef said quietly, "I didn't need a plan, I needed you to just sit here." Lars felt his face burn. He went to the university's study support office the next day and set up a weekly planning session. And that evening he knocked on Yosef's door, sat on the floor and said nothing for a long time. Yosef passed him a cup of tea.

qa.q: Why did Lars miss the exam registration deadline?
qa.a: The email sat unread among two hundred others.

qa.q: How did Lars feel when Yosef said he just needed company?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and ashamed, his face burning as he realised he had missed what Yosef needed.

qa.q: How did Lars work on his gaps without giving up on himself?
qa.a: He went to study support for weekly planning, and he returned to Yosef to simply sit with him.

qa.q: What was it like for Yosef when Lars came and sat quietly?
qa.a: Yosef likely felt comforted and cared for, which he showed by passing Lars a cup of tea.

grounding: Shows a young adult brilliant at analysis who struggles with organisation and emotional skills at once, facing both without shame and working on each.

passage: At the college hackathon, Jatin, nineteen, cracked the routing algorithm at 3 a.m. that had stumped every team. At 5 a.m. he discovered he'd saved it nowhere. His teammate Aditi found him staring at the screen. "It's gone. I'm useless," he said. Aditi, the team lead, had been tired and snappy herself all night, and he hadn't noticed. She sat down. "You're brilliant at the hard part, and you're terrible at saving files. Both are true. Rewrite it; I'll set up auto-save." He rewrote it in forty minutes. Later, he said, "You were upset last night, weren't you? I missed that." Aditi smiled. "You're learning." They came second, and Jatin kept a sticky note on his laptop: SAVE. ASK.

qa.q: What did Jatin write on his sticky note?
qa.a: He wrote SAVE. ASK.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel when he found his work was not saved?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and hopeless, calling himself useless.

qa.q: How did Aditi help Jatin see his strengths and gaps without shame?
qa.a: She named both honestly, that he is brilliant at algorithms and bad at saving files, then helped fix the practical gap.

qa.q: How might Aditi feel when Jatin asks about her mood?
qa.a: She may feel noticed and pleased, seeing that he is working on reading other people's feelings.

grounding: Shows a young adult with brilliant analysis but weak organisation and emotional awareness, helped to see both without shame and work on each.

passage: Back from the zoo in Mysuru, Shankar, five, burst through the flat door. "Amma! Th-th-th-the elephant, it, it, it squirted water on a man!" His eyes squeezed tight on the "th," his cheeks tense. He didn't seem to notice; the story kept pouring out. Payal, his mother, knelt to his height and kept looking at him, not rushing. She didn't finish his sentence, though she could guess it. "Really? On a man? What did the man do?" "He, he, he jumped!" Shankar shouted, laughing, and hopped across the room to show her. She laughed with him.

qa.q: What did the elephant do at the zoo?
qa.a: The elephant squirted water on a man.

qa.q: How was Shankar feeling as he told the story?
qa.a: He was excited and happy, so eager to share that he did not seem to notice the repeated sounds.

qa.q: What did Payal do that helped Shankar keep talking?
qa.a: She knelt, kept looking at him, waited calmly and did not finish his sentence, then asked about his story.

qa.q: What would change if Payal had kept finishing Shankar's sentences?
qa.a: Shankar might start to feel his way of talking was wrong and share his stories less.

grounding: Shows a child who repeats sounds when excited, with some facial tension, who seems unaware of it, and a parent who listens calmly without finishing his sentences.

passage:
"Paaaapa! Papa, the p-p-p-puppy at school, it, it licked my hand!"
Francis put down the vegetables. "It licked your hand? Which puppy?"
"The b-b-brown one. It has one white ear."
"One white ear! Did it have a name?"
Disha screwed up her face. "Mmmmmm. Mmmmango!"
"Mango! That's a great name."
"Mmmm, Miss said we can bring it, bring it a biscuit tomorrow."
"Then we'll find a biscuit tonight."
Disha danced around the kitchen, singing "Mango, Mango." Francis smiled and went back to chopping.

qa.q: What was the puppy's name?
qa.a: The puppy's name was Mango.

qa.q: How was Disha feeling when she told Papa about the puppy?
qa.a: She was very excited and happy, dancing around the kitchen afterward.

qa.q: What did Francis do that fitted a child who stretches and repeats sounds?
qa.a: He stopped what he was doing, listened calmly, never finished her words or told her to slow down, and asked about her story.

qa.q: What might it be like for Francis to hear about Mango?
qa.a: Francis probably enjoys Disha's excitement and feels close to her, happy to share her news about the puppy.

grounding: Shows a child who repeats and stretches sounds when excited, and a parent who listens calmly without finishing her sentences.

passage:
Show-and-tell note, Nursery B, Friday.
Uday, five, brought a seashell from his holiday. Excited, he said, "I-I-I-I found it in the, the, the ssssand," his lips pressed tight on the S. He seemed unaware and kept talking. Two children started to call out the word for him. I raised a hand; they waited. I kept looking at Uday and let him finish. He held the shell to each child's ear.
I told his father calmly at pickup that we listen without finishing his sentences, and that a speech therapist can advise if they ever want. — Gopika

qa.q: What did Uday bring for show-and-tell?
qa.a: He brought a seashell from his holiday.

qa.q: How was Uday feeling during show-and-tell?
qa.a: He was excited and proud of his shell, and did not seem aware of repeating sounds.

qa.q: What did Gopika do that helped Uday during his turn?
qa.a: Gopika signalled the children to wait, kept looking at Uday and let him finish his own words.

qa.q: How might Uday's father feel after hearing Gopika at pickup?
qa.a: He may feel reassured by the calm tone and grateful to know where to get advice if needed.

grounding: Shows a child repeating and stretching sounds when excited, largely unaware, and a teacher who listens calmly and stops others finishing his sentences.

passage: I'm Gurleen, from the flat next door. Tejas, five, rang my bell with a broken kite. "G-G-G-Gurleen, the k-k-kite, it, it..." His face went tight. I waited, looking at him. I didn't say "slow down"; my own uncle stutters, and says that makes it worse. "It fell off the r-roof and the string broke." "Oh no. Shall we fix it?" We sat on my steps with tape. Later his uncle said, "Tejas, take a breath first," and Tejas went quiet. I can't know what he felt, but later he told me all about the pigeon the kite nearly hit.

qa.q: What was wrong with Tejas's kite?
qa.a: It fell off the roof and the string broke.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling while waiting for Tejas to finish?
qa.a: Gurleen felt patient and caring, keen not to rush him, knowing from a relative how "slow down" can hurt.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do that respected Tejas's pace?
qa.a: Gurleen waited, kept looking at him, did not finish his words or tell him to slow down, and answered what he actually said.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt when his uncle said "take a breath first"?
qa.a: He may have felt embarrassed or corrected, since he went quiet and stopped talking.

grounding: Shows an adult neighbour who waits, does not complete a stuttering child's sentences or tell him to slow down, and treats him as a full conversation partner.

passage:
Monday: During the animal game, Francis, five, said, "M-m-m-my one is a f-f-f..." Shreya shouted, "Frog!" Francis frowned. "No. Fox." He didn't talk for the rest of the game.
Wednesday: Their teacher read a story about a boy whose words came slowly, and the class talked about waiting for friends. Shreya listened with her chin on her knees.
Friday: At the sand tray Francis began, "My n-n-n-nani has a, a, a g-g-goat." Shreya waited, watching him, her mouth shut tight. "It ate her slipper!" Shreya squealed. "Tell me more!" Francis told her all about the goat until the bell.

qa.q: What animal did Francis actually mean on Monday?
qa.a: He meant a fox.

qa.q: How did Shreya seem to feel on Friday while waiting for Francis?
qa.a: She seemed patient and interested, working hard to keep quiet, then delighted by the goat story.

qa.q: What helped Shreya change how she listened?
qa.a: Hearing the story about waiting for friends to finish helped her learn not to guess Francis's words.

qa.q: How was Francis affected on Monday compared with Friday?
qa.a: On Monday he felt frustrated and stopped talking; on Friday he felt heard and told the whole goat story.

grounding: Shows a young peer learning to wait and not complete a stuttering friend's sentences, and treating him as a full conversation partner.

passage: The school van was already honking downstairs when Hafsa, five, grabbed her aunt's hand. "Kashish Khala, I d-d-d-dreamt a, a, a b-b-b..." Kashish wanted to rush; the driver was waving from the window. She bent down anyway and kept her eyes on Hafsa's. She didn't guess the word. She didn't say "take a breath." "...b-b-blue whale in our b-bathtub!" Kashish's mouth fell open. "A whale in the bathtub! How did it fit?" "It, it, it was a baby one," Hafsa said, very serious. Kashish laughed. "Tell me the rest after school, okay?" Hafsa nodded hard and ran for the van.

qa.q: What did Hafsa dream about?
qa.a: She dreamt about a blue whale in their bathtub.

qa.q: How might Kashish have felt with the van honking?
qa.a: She probably felt rushed and pressured, wanting to hurry, but chose to stay patient.

qa.q: What did Kashish do that respected Hafsa's pace?
qa.a: She bent down, kept eye contact, did not guess words or say "take a breath," and responded to the story with real interest.

qa.q: How might Hafsa have felt running for the van?
qa.a: Hafsa likely felt happy and listened to, looking forward to finishing the story after school.

grounding: Shows an adult who, despite time pressure, waits, does not finish a stuttering child's words or tell her to breathe, and treats her as a full partner.

passage: In the government school near Hassan, Madhuri, ten, counted the rows ahead of her during reading time, working out which paragraph would be hers. It started with "Monday." She practised under her breath: "The first day of the week." Her stomach twisted. When Kashish, at the next desk, copied her stutter at lunch, Madhuri stopped talking altogether for a week. Her teacher, Shobha Ma'am, noticed. She told Kashish firmly that mocking was not allowed, and told Madhuri, "You can take as long as you need. We will wait." Twice a month, a speech therapist visited the primary health centre, and Madhuri's mother began taking her there. Slowly, reading time became something she could face.

qa.q: How did Madhuri plan to avoid saying "Monday"?
qa.a: She planned to say "The first day of the week" instead.

qa.q: How did Madhuri feel during reading time?
qa.a: She felt afraid and dreaded it, counting rows ahead and feeling her stomach twist.

qa.q: What steps helped Madhuri?
qa.a: Her teacher stopped the mocking and gave her time, and she began seeing a speech therapist at the primary health centre.

qa.q: How might Kashish's copying have affected Madhuri?
qa.a: It made things worse, hurting and shaming her so much that she stopped talking for a week.

grounding: Shows a child who dreads reading aloud and swaps words to avoid sounds, made worse by teasing, and helped by a patient teacher and a speech therapist.

passage: In Durban, Zanele, eleven, woke with a stomach ache every Thursday: oral report day. She wrote her talks full of easy words, "talk" instead of "presentation," "big" instead of "enormous," because P and E sounds got stuck. When a boy laughed at her last time, she wanted to disappear. On Tuesday afternoons she saw Siddiq, a speech therapist at the community clinic, who helped her practise gently and never mocked. This week her teacher, Mrs Dube, said, "Zanele, you can go last, and take all the time you need." Zanele spoke for three minutes about her grandmother's garden. She stuck on "tomatoes" twice. Nobody laughed. She sat down with her hands still shaking, but smiling.

qa.q: On which afternoons did Zanele see Siddiq?
qa.a: She saw Siddiq on Tuesday afternoons.

qa.q: How did Zanele feel about oral report day?
qa.a: She dreaded it and felt afraid, waking with a stomach ache every Thursday.

qa.q: What helped Zanele give her report?
qa.a: Practice with a qualified speech therapist, and a teacher who let her go last and take all the time she needed.

qa.q: How might Mrs Dube feel watching Zanele sit down smiling?
qa.a: Mrs Dube may feel glad and proud that giving Zanele time helped her get through the report.

grounding: Shows a child who dreads speaking, swaps words to dodge sounds and is hurt by teasing, and is helped by a teacher allowing time and speech therapy.

passage: At roll call in Class 4, Pallavi, nine, never said "Present." She said "Yes, Ma'am," because the P got stuck. On reading days she had tummy aches and asked to go to the sick room. Reena Ma'am noticed the pattern. One morning she kept Pallavi back after assembly. "Would you like to read your part to me alone first, before class?" Pallavi nodded, eyes on her shoes. When she read in class later and a boy sniggered, Reena Ma'am said, "We wait for everyone here," and waited with the class. Pallavi also started Saturday sessions with a speech therapist her parents found through the school. By the end of term, she said "Present" once. Quietly, but she said it.

qa.q: What did Pallavi say instead of "Present" at roll call?
qa.a: She said "Yes, Ma'am."

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel on reading days?
qa.a: She felt fearful and anxious, getting tummy aches and asking to go to the sick room.

qa.q: What did Reena Ma'am do to make speaking less frightening?
qa.a: She let Pallavi read to her alone first, stopped the sniggering and made the whole class wait patiently.

qa.q: How might Pallavi's parents feel when she says "Present" at last?
qa.a: They may feel proud and hopeful, seeing the speech therapy and teacher support begin to help.

grounding: Shows a child who swaps words, avoids reading aloud and dreads being called on, helped by a patient teacher who stops teasing and by a speech therapist.

passage: Salma, sixteen, had the answer to the chemistry question before anyone else. She could see it, clear as a formula on the board. She kept her hand down. At home in Hyderabad, when Ammi asked her to call the gas agency, she pretended to be busy until her sister Parveen did it. She rehearsed even simple lines in her head: "One refill, please, for flat 3B." Last month a shopkeeper had smirked while she was stuck on "refill," and she still felt it in her chest. That night Parveen sat beside her. "Your words take longer. Your brain doesn't." Salma swallowed. "It's not the words. It's their faces." Parveen squeezed her hand. "Then let's practise the gas call together, with my face."

qa.q: What line did Salma rehearse for the gas call?
qa.a: She rehearsed "One refill, please, for flat 3B."

qa.q: What does Salma mean when she says "It's their faces"?
qa.a: She feels ashamed and anxious mainly about how people react, like the shopkeeper's smirk, more than about the stutter itself.

qa.q: What step does Parveen offer that could help Salma?
qa.a: She offers to practise the gas call together, so Salma can rehearse with a safe, kind listener.

qa.q: How does Parveen see Salma's ability?
qa.a: She sees that Salma's thinking is quick and clear; only the words take longer to come out.

grounding: Shows a teenager who stays silent, avoids phone calls and rehearses constantly despite clear thoughts, whose stress comes mostly from how others react.

passage:
"Uma, the debate trials are tomorrow. Why didn't you sign up?"
"You know why, Nandini."
"You have the best arguments in class. You wrote my whole rebuttal last year."
"In my head, they're perfect. I've rehearsed every one about fifty times."
"So say them."
"And watch everyone's faces when I get stuck on 'however'? The judges looking at their watches?"
"So it's not the talking. It's them."
Uma nodded, picking at the strap of her bag. "Last year a boy laughed. I still hear it."
"Then I'll sit in the front row. Look at me, not the judges."
Uma was quiet a long time. "You'd really do that?"
"I'd really do that. Sign up."

qa.q: What did Uma write for Nandini last year?
qa.a: She wrote Nandini's whole rebuttal last year.

qa.q: What is Uma most worried about?
qa.a: She is anxious and ashamed about people's reactions, the faces, the judges and a laugh she still remembers, not about her arguments.

qa.q: How does Nandini help Uma face the trials?
qa.a: She points out that the problem is others' reactions, and offers to sit in the front row as a friendly face to look at.

qa.q: How does Nandini see Uma's abilities?
qa.a: Nandini sees her as having the best arguments in class, someone who is already a strong debater in thought.

grounding: Shows a teenager who rehearses constantly and stays silent though her thoughts are ready, whose stress is mostly about how others react.

passage: At seventeen I would do almost anything to avoid a phone call. My name is Maria, and I stutter, mostly on M, which is unlucky. I once walked two kilometres in the rain to a pizza place rather than phone in an order. In class my answers were ready, full sentences, but I'd shrug and say "I don't know." At night I rehearsed tomorrow's conversations, word by word. My cousin Tanuja noticed. "You're not scared of talking," she said. "You're scared of people waiting." She was right. The worst part was never the stuck sound. It was the sigh from the other end of the phone. Knowing that didn't fix everything, but it helped me stop blaming myself.

qa.q: How far did Maria walk to avoid phoning in an order?
qa.a: Maria walked two kilometres in the rain to a pizza place.

qa.q: What was Maria most afraid of, according to Tanuja?
qa.a: Maria was afraid and ashamed of people waiting and reacting, like the sigh on the phone, not of talking itself.

qa.q: How did Tanuja's comment help Maria?
qa.a: It showed Maria that the real stress came from others' reactions, which helped Maria stop self-blame.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt watching Maria avoid calls and answers?
qa.a: Tanuja may have felt concerned and protective, noticing how much effort the avoidance was costing.

grounding: Shows a teenager who avoids calls, stays silent and rehearses despite clear thoughts, realising the stress is mostly about others' reactions.

passage:
First week of college: at the photography club, Joseph stood up to introduce himself. His throat locked on the J. He paused, then said, "I stutter, so give me a second. J-Joseph. I shoot street photos." Nobody laughed. Ira, in the front, kept looking at him, waiting.
Third week: Joseph presented his street series. He slowed down on purpose, stuck on "market" twice, and didn't say sorry once. Ira asked the first question.
Sixth week: Joseph went to a stuttering support group at the city library. Eight people sat in a circle, trading stories about phone calls and job interviews. For the first time, he didn't feel like the only one. He walked out laughing with a man who stuttered on every B.

qa.q: What does Joseph photograph?
qa.a: He shoots street photos.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel at the support group?
qa.a: He felt less alone and relieved, laughing with another member and no longer feeling like the only one.

qa.q: What did Joseph do that shows confident speaking?
qa.a: He named his stutter openly, slowed down on purpose and did not apologise during his presentation.

qa.q: How did Ira's behaviour help Joseph?
qa.a: Ira kept eye contact, waited patiently and asked the first question, treating Joseph as a normal speaker.

grounding: Shows a young adult speaking openly about stuttering, slowing down without apology, helped by a patient listener and a support group.

passage: "Nilesh, sit, sit. You're worried about Monday's client pitch because of your stutter? Let me tell you something. When I was twenty-two, in my first job at the bank, I stuttered so badly I used to hide in the store room when the phone rang. My first presentation, I apologised eleven times. My manager, Mr D'Souza, stopped me after. He said, 'Yogesh, stop saying sorry. Just say it slowly. We'll wait.' And he did. He looked me in the eye every time. A colleague told me about a stuttering group that met at a temple hall on Sundays. I went, terrified. Twenty people like me! After that I started every meeting saying, 'I stutter, bear with me.' Never apologised again. So, Monday, you slow down. I'll be in the room."

qa.q: How many times did Yogesh apologise in his first presentation?
qa.a: He apologised eleven times.

qa.q: How did young Yogesh feel going to the stuttering group for the first time?
qa.a: He felt terrified at first, then surprised and relieved to find twenty people like him.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Yogesh spoke?
qa.a: His manager told him to stop apologising and slow down while he waited and kept eye contact, and Yogesh then found a support group.

qa.q: How might Mr D'Souza have seen young Yogesh?
qa.a: He likely saw a capable young employee worth waiting for, not someone who needed to apologise.

grounding: An elder recalls learning to speak openly about stuttering, slow down without apologising, helped by a patient manager and a support group.

passage: The interview panel was running late, and the coordinator told Hemant, twenty-two, "You'll only get ten minutes, sorry." His heart sank; ten minutes felt like nothing for someone who stutters. He walked in and sat down. "Before we start, I stutter. I'll take my time, and I'll get there." The main interviewer, Ritu, nodded and kept her eyes on him. When he stuck on "project," she waited. He didn't apologise. He explained his water-sensor design clearly, slowly, point by point. At the end Ritu said, "That was the clearest explanation today." Outside, he texted his support group: "Did it. Didn't say sorry once." Three replies came back in a minute.

qa.q: How many minutes did the coordinator say Hemant would get?
qa.a: The coordinator said he would only get ten minutes.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel when told he would get only ten minutes?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and worried, his heart sinking, since he stutters and the time felt short.

qa.q: What choices helped Hemant speak with confidence?
qa.a: He named his stutter at the start, took his time and did not apologise, explaining his design point by point.

qa.q: How did Ritu see Hemant's explanation?
qa.a: Ritu found it the clearest explanation of the day, and she showed respect by waiting and keeping eye contact.

grounding: Shows a young adult who speaks openly about stuttering and does not apologise, helped by a patient listener and a support group, despite time pressure.
